transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what’s been bothering me is I feel like I’m always up and moving, even when there’s no real reason to be. Like on a quiet day, I’ll start with the garden club list, then suddenly I’m at my knitting bag, and then I remember the travel papers I meant to look at—oh, and those are in a folder somewhere, I think by the phone—and before I know it I haven’t really finished any one thing. It’s like I’m just bouncing from one thing to the next.
Has this feeling of being unable to focus and jumping between tasks been something you've experienced most of your life, or is it a new change from how you usually are?

Oh, no, it’s not new. I mean, I think I’ve always been like that, in one way or another. Even back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother I was bright but, you know, scattered. I’d lose papers, talk before I was supposed to, and I remember wiggling in my seat when I was meant to be finishing my work.

Funny, my mother kept some of those old school things in a box for years—though I don’t know what happened to that box now. But yes, it goes way back.

Aside from this lifelong pattern, have you ever had a distinct period—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, with more energy than usual, that was different from how you normally feel?

I’m not sure I’d call it elevated or euphoric, no. I mean, I have days where I’m busy and I get a lot of ideas going—like when I start reorganizing the pantry and then somehow end up sorting old greeting cards—but that feels more like my usual way of being, not some separate spell that lasts for days.

I don’t think I’ve had a period that was really different like that, at least not that I can think of.
Would you say these patterns of losing focus and jumping between tasks have caused real problems for you in more than one area of your life—like at work, at home, or in your relationships?

Yes, I think so. It’s not just me being a little forgetful around the house anymore. My husband gets frustrated because he can’t really count on me to keep plans straight unless he checks behind me.

And at the community center too—oh, I was helping with a sign-up sheet there, and then I meant to call someone about the room setup, but I got sidetracked by another list—I suppose that’s the sort of thing. The other volunteers are kind about it, mostly, but I can tell they don’t really trust me to keep everything organized on my own. It’s embarrassing.
